options: The fewest customers needed to support a business
The farthest distance people will travel to shop
The point at which a town grows into a city
The number of goods offered in each settlement
questions.explanation: The professor defines threshold as the minimum number of customers needed to keep a business going.

questions.explanation: The professor says circles would overlap or leave gaps, while hexagons fit together perfectly.

questions.explanation: He notes the unrealistic assumptions but says the hierarchy remains surprisingly visible.

intro: Listen to a talk in a history of technology class.
talk: We often credit Johannes Gutenberg with inventing movable type around 1450. But that's not quite right. Movable type was first invented in China, in the 1040s, by a craftsman named Bi Sheng, who made individual characters out of baked clay. And in Korea, printers were using movable metal type by the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The oldest surviving book printed with metal type is Korean, from 1377, decades before Gutenberg. So here's the question. Why did movable type transform European society so quickly, while in East Asia it remained less dominant? One major factor is the writing system. European languages use alphabets with a few dozen letters. Chinese writing uses thousands of characters. A printer working in Chinese needed an enormous stock of type, and finding and sorting each character was slow. Woodblock printing, where an entire page is carved into a single block, was often simply more practical. The blocks could be stored and reused for new print runs. So it's a mistake to see East Asia as having missed an opportunity. Printers there made a reasonable choice, and woodblock printing produced enormous numbers of books. Gutenberg's real achievement, then, wasn't the idea of movable type. It was a whole system: a mold for casting identical metal letters quickly, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from those used to make wine.

intro: Listen to a talk in a world history class.
talk: The Inca Empire, stretching along the Andes, ran a huge state, with roads, storehouses, and labor obligations, all without writing in the usual sense. So how did they keep records? The answer is the quipu, a set of knotted cords. A quipu has a main cord, with dozens or even hundreds of cords hanging from it. On many quipus, the knots record numbers in a base-ten system. Knots farthest from the main cord represent units, the next cluster up represents tens, then hundreds, and so on. Different types of knots made the system readable; for example, a figure-eight knot marks a one in the units position. This code was worked out in the early twentieth century, and it shows quipus were used for census counts and tribute records. The officials who made and read them were specialists. Now, here's the open question. Spanish chroniclers after the conquest reported that these specialists could recite histories, laws, and family lines from their cords. So did some quipus record language, not just numbers? A significant share of surviving quipus don't seem to fit the numerical system, and features like color, fiber, and knot direction may carry meaning. But no one has deciphered them. One problem is that the chroniclers may have misunderstood what they saw. Another is that the cords may have been memory aids, readable only by their makers.

intro: Listen to a talk in a history of science class.
talk: In the mid-1800s, most doctors in Europe believed that diseases like cholera spread through miasma, which basically means bad air, foul smells rising from rotting matter. It made sense: disease was common in crowded, smelly neighborhoods. But the London doctor John Snow suspected that cholera spread through contaminated water. In 1854, a severe outbreak struck the Soho district of London, and hundreds of people died within days. Snow went door to door, recording where the victims had lived, and he marked the deaths on a map. They clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. Now, some of the most persuasive evidence came from the exceptions. A nearby brewery had almost no cases. Why? The workers were given beer to drink, and the brewery had its own well, so they didn't use the pump. A nearby workhouse, also with its own well, had very few deaths. Meanwhile, a woman who lived miles away had died. It turned out she liked the taste of Broad Street water and had it brought to her house. Snow presented his findings, and local officials removed the handle of the pump. It's a famous story, but one caution: the outbreak was already declining by then, partly because many residents had fled. So removing the handle probably wasn't what ended it. The real importance was the method: careful mapping and close attention to exceptions.

intro: Listen to a talk in a painting class.
talk: When we talk about Impressionism, we usually talk about artists like Monet and Renoir and their interest in capturing light outdoors. But today I want to look at a humble piece of technology that helped make that possible: the paint tube. Before the 1840s, oil paint was hard to carry around. Painters, or their assistants, ground pigments by hand and mixed them with oil in the studio. If paint was stored at all, it was usually kept in small bags made from pig bladders, tied with string. You'd prick the bladder to squeeze out some paint, but the bags leaked, burst easily, and the paint dried out. Then, in 1841, an American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented a collapsible metal tube with a cap. Paint stayed fresh, and it could be carried anywhere. Combined with portable easels and a range of new, bright, ready-made colors, this meant painters could work outdoors, directly in front of the scene, for hours. Renoir is reported to have said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Now, we shouldn't overstate this. Artists had been making small oil sketches outdoors long before tubes existed. And many Impressionist paintings that look spontaneous were actually reworked or finished in the studio. So the tube didn't create the movement. But it certainly made the Impressionists' way of working far easier.

intro: Listen to a talk in a music history class.
talk: Today let's talk about an instrument you all know, whose name tells a story. Around 1700, in Florence, an instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori, who worked for the powerful Medici family, built a new kind of keyboard. Now, the dominant keyboard instrument at the time was the harpsichord. When you press a harpsichord key, a small quill plucks the string. And here's the limitation: no matter how hard or softly you press the key, the string is plucked in much the same way, so the volume barely changes. Cristofori's idea was to strike the strings with small hammers instead. The harder you press the key, the faster the hammer moves, and the louder the sound. He also solved a tricky mechanical problem: the hammer had to hit the string and then immediately fall away, so the string could keep vibrating. He called the instrument, roughly translated, a harpsichord with soft and loud, in Italian, piano e forte. And that's where our word piano comes from. Interestingly, the invention didn't catch on right away. It took decades of improvements before the piano became the instrument that composers like Mozart and Beethoven wrote for. There was one older keyboard that could vary its volume, by the way: the clavichord. But it was so quiet that it was mainly used for practice in small rooms, not for public performance.

intro: Listen to a talk in an anthropology class.
talk: We tend to imagine life before farming as a constant struggle for survival, people working from dawn to dusk just to eat. In the 1960s, the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins challenged that picture with a deliberately provocative phrase: the original affluent society. His argument drew on new studies of foragers, people who live by hunting and gathering, including groups in the Kalahari Desert. Researchers had recorded how much time people actually spent getting food, and the numbers were surprisingly low, often around fifteen to twenty hours a week. So in what sense were they affluent? Sahlins pointed out that there are two ways to satisfy your wants. You can produce a lot, or you can want little. Foragers moved often, so owning many things was a burden, not a benefit. With modest wants and fairly reliable food sources, they had plenty of leisure. Now, the critique. Later anthropologists pointed out that those early figures counted only time spent hunting and gathering. They left out making tools, processing food, collecting firewood, and other household work. Include all of that, and the total comes much closer to a full working week. Studies also found seasonal hunger in some groups. So the strong version of Sahlins's claim hasn't held up. But his deeper point, that affluence depends on what people want, not only on what they have, still challenges ideas of economic progress.
